'''Arm Holdings plc''' is a British [[semiconductor]] and [[computer software|software]] design [[company]] headquartered in [[Cambridge]], England, whose primary business is the design of [[central processing unit]] (CPU) cores that implement the [[ARM architecture family]] of [[Instruction set architecture|instruction sets]]. It also designs other chips, provides [[software development tools]] under the DS-5, RealView and [[Keil (company)|Keil]] brands, and provides [[platform (computing)|systems and platforms]], [[system-on-chip]] (SoC) infrastructure and software. As a [[holding company]], it also holds shares of other companies. Since 2016, it has been majority owned by Japanese conglomerate [[SoftBank Group]].

"ARM" was originally an acronym for [[Acorn Computers|Acorn RISC Machine]] and later for Advanced [[Reduced instruction set computer|RISC]] Machines. While ARM CPUs first appeared in the [[Acorn Archimedes]], a [[desktop computer]], today's systems include mostly [[embedded system]]s, including ARM CPUs used in virtually all modern [[smartphone]]s. Processors based on designs licensed from Arm, or designed by licensees of one of the [[ARM architecture family|ARM instruction set architectures]], are used in all classes of computing devices. Arm has two lines of [[graphics processing unit]]s (GPUs), [[Mali (processor)|Mali]], and the newer [[Immortalis (GPU)|Immortalis]] (which includes hardware-based [[ray tracing (graphics)|ray-tracing]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schoon |first=Ben |date=28 June 2022 |title=Arm's new Immortalis GPU sets the stage for more Android phones with ray-tracing support |url=https://9to5google.com/2022/06/28/arm-immortalis-gpu-ray-tracing-android/ |access-date=7 July 2022 |website=[[9to5Google]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

Arm's main CPU competitors in servers include [[IBM]], [[Intel]] and [[AMD]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.eetimes.com/cavium-flexes-arm-server-upgrade/ |title=Cavium Flexes ARM Server Upgrade |first=Rick |last=Merritt |date=30 May 2016 |website=[[EE Times]]}}</ref> Intel competed with ARM-based chips in mobile devices but Arm no longer has any competition in that space (although vendors of actual ARM-based chips compete within that arena). Arm's main GPU competitors include mobile GPUs from technology companies [[Imagination Technologies]] ([[PowerVR]]), [[Qualcomm]] ([[Adreno]]), and increasingly [[Nvidia]], [[AMD]], [[Samsung]] and [[Intel]]. While competing in GPUs, Qualcomm, Samsung and Nvidia all have combined their GPUs with Arm-licensed CPUs.

Arm had a primary listing on the [[London Stock Exchange]] (LSE) and was a constituent of the [[FTSE 100 Index]]. It also had a secondary listing of [[American depositary receipt]]s on New York's [[Nasdaq]]. ==History==
{{See also|ARM architecture family#History}}

===Name===
The acronym ARM was first used in 1983 and originally stood for "Acorn RISC Machine". [[Acorn Computers]]' first [[reduced instruction set computing|RISC]] processor was used in the original [[Acorn Archimedes]] and was one of the first RISC processors used in small computers. However, when the company was incorporated in 1990, what 'ARM' stood for changed to "Advanced RISC Machines". According to [[Steve Furber]] the name was changed at the behest of Apple, which did not wish to have the name of a competitor in the name of the company. At the time of the [[initial public offering|IPO]] in 1998, the company name was changed to "ARM Holdings",<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://quotes.nasdaq.com/asp/SummaryQuote.asp?symbol=ARMH&selected=ARMH |title=Company Description (as filed with the SEC) |publisher=NASDAQ |access-date=18 April 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110505072606/http://quotes.nasdaq.com/asp/SummaryQuote.asp?symbol=ARMH&selected=ARMH |archive-date=5 May 2011 }}</ref> often just called ARM like the processors.<ref name=companieshouse>{{cite web |url= https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/02557590|title=Arm Limited| publisher=Companies House|access-date=13 February 2022}}</ref>

On 1 August 2017, the styling and [[logo]] were changed. The logo is now all lowercase ('arm') and other uses of the name are in sentence case ('Arm').<ref name="companieshouse" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://linuxgizmos.com/arm-becomes-arm-or-is-it-arm/ |title=Chip IP designer ARM becomes 'Arm' – or is it arm? |date=7 August 2017 |first= Eric| last= Brown |website=LinuxGizmos.com }}</ref>

===Founding===
The company was founded on 12 November 1990 as '''Widelogic Limited''' but this was rapidly changed, on 3 December 1990, to '''Advanced RISC Machines Limited''' and structured as a [[joint venture]] between [[Acorn Computers]], [[Apple Inc.|Apple]], and [[VLSI Technology]]. Acorn provided 12 employees, VLSI provided tools, Apple provided a US$3 million investment (equivalent to ${{Inflation|index=USD|value=3|start_year=1990}} million in {{Inflation/year|index=USD}}).<ref The new company intended to further the development of the [[ARM architecture family|Acorn RISC Machine]] processor, which was originally used in the Acorn Archimedes and had been selected by Apple for its [[Apple Newton|Newton]] project. Its first profitable year was 1993. The company's Silicon Valley and Tokyo offices were opened in 1994. ARM invested in Palmchip Corporation in 1997 to provide system on chip platforms and to enter into the disk drive market.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.eetimes.com/document.asp?doc_id=1210443|title=PALMCHIP Introduces Fully-Integrated, Low-Power Controller Core for OEM Mass Storage Design|date=16 May 1997|work=EE Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.arm.com/about/company-profile/milestones.php?fullsite=yes|title=ARM Company Milestones|website= arm.com | publisher= ARM Holdings| access-date= }}</ref> In 1998, the company changed its name from ''Advanced RISC Machines Ltd'' to ''ARM Ltd''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m0EIN/is_/ai_53093087 |title=Advanced RISC Machines Ltd is now ARM Ltd | website= Findarticles.com |date=19 October 1998 |access-date=18 April 2011}}</ref> The company was first listed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) and [[Nasdaq]] in 1998<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m0CGN/is_/ai_20505833 |title=ARM wins billion dollar valuation in IPO |publisher=Findarticles.com |date=20 April 1998 |access-date=18 April 2011}}</ref> and by February 1999, Apple's shareholding had fallen to 14.8 per cent.<ref name="cnet short take">{{cite news | url=http://news.cnet.com/Short-Take-Apple-sells-ARM-shares/2110-1001_3-221149.html | title=Short Take: Apple sells ARM shares | work=CNET.com | date=3 February 1999 | access-date=6 February 2012 | last= Davis| first= Jim | quote=Apple still holds 14.8 percent of ARM [...]}}</ref>

In 2010, ARM joined with [[IBM]], [[Texas Instruments]], [[Samsung]], [[ST-Ericsson]] (since dissolved) and [[Freescale Semiconductor]] (now [[NXP Semiconductors]]) in forming a [[nonprofit organization|non-profit]] [[Open-source software|open source]] engineering company, [[Linaro]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dailytech.com/IBM+Freescale+Samsung+Form+Linaro+to+Aid+in+Developing+ARMcompatible+Software/article18611.htm |title=IBM, Freescale, Samsung Form Linaro to Aid in Developing ARM-compatible Software |first=Shane |last=McGlaun |website=Daily Tech |date=3 June 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170801120716/http://www.dailytech.com/IBM+Freescale+Samsung+Form+Linaro+to+Aid+in+Developing+ARMcompatible+Software/article18611.htm |archive-date=1 August 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

From 2020, discord between Arm and the effective owners of Arm China became visible after the British parent company unsuccessfully tried to oust the chief executive of the subsidiary, who, however, managed to retain his position.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Inside the battle for Arm China|work= Financial Times| first1= Henny| last1= Sender |first2= Kana| last2= Inagaki| first3= Ryan| last3= McMorrow |first4= Nian| last4= Liu |first5= Nic |last5= Fildes | url=https://www.ft.com/content/dc55d4c9-1065-4db0-98a4-f7f0c1de563b| date= June 26, 2020| access-date= February 7, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=How SoftBank's sale of Arm China sowed the seeds of discord |url= https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/China-tech/How-SoftBank-s-sale-of-Arm-China-sowed-the-seeds-of-discord|access-date=4 September 2021|website=[[Nikkei Asia]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> A prevailing view emerged that the matter would negatively affect the pending approval by the Chinese regulators of the SoftBank–Nvidia deal, as well as any [[public offering]] of Arm.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Battle at Arm China threatens $40bn Nvidia deal |url= https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Technology/Battle-at-Arm-China-threatens-40bn-Nvidia-deal|access-date=11 June 2021|website=Nikkei Asia|language=en-GB|archive-date=11 June 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210611050712/https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Technology/Battle-at-Arm-China-threatens-40bn-Nvidia-deal|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Gross |first1=Anna |last2=Bradshaw |first2=Tim |last3= McMorrow |first3=Ryan |date=11 February 2022 |title=SoftBank's plans for Arm IPO hit by legal battle over renegade China unit |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/8494d5f3-4f3e-4a1d-878d-cabb82e37778 |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref>

==Operations==
Unlike most traditional microprocessor suppliers, such as [[Intel]], [[Freescale]] (the former semiconductor division of [[Motorola]], now [[NXP Semiconductors]]) and [[Renesas]] (a former joint venture between [[Hitachi]] and [[Mitsubishi Electric]]), ARM only creates and licenses its technology as [[Semiconductor intellectual property|intellectual property]] (IP),<ref>{{cite web| url= https://www.arm.com/products/processors/licensees.php|title=Processor Licensees|publisher=ARM Limited}}</ref> rather than manufacturing and selling its own physical [[Central processing unit|CPU]]s, GPUs, SoCs or microcontrollers. This model is similar to those of fellow British design houses [[Synopsys#ARC International|ARC International]] and [[Imagination Technologies]], which have similarly been designing and licensing GPUs, CPUs, and SoCs, along with supplying tooling and various design and support services to its licensees.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-50976759|title=Imagination announces new Apple licence deal|date=2 January 2020|publisher=BBC|access-date=13 February 2022}}</ref>

Cray already has one customer lined up for the ThunderX2-powered XC50: the Great Western 4 (GW4) Alliance, a research consortium of four UK universities (Bristol, Bath, Cardiff and Exeter). In January 2017, the alliance announced it had contracted Cray to build "Isambard," a 10,000-core ARM-based supercomputer, which will provide a Tier 2 HPC service. Fujitsu (the supercomputer maker of June 2011 world's fastest [[K computer]] according to [[TOP500]]) announced at the [[International Supercomputing Conference]] in June 2016 that its future [[Exascale computing|exascale]] supercomputer will feature processors of its own design that implement the [[ARMv8]] architecture, rather than the [[SPARC]] processors used in earlier supercomputers. ==Licensees==
Companies often license these designs from Arm to manufacture and integrate into their own [[System on a chip|''System on chip'']] (SoC) with other components such as [[graphics processing unit|GPU]]s (sometimes Arm's Mali) or [[modem]]/[[Baseband processor|radio basebands]] (for mobile phones). Arm offers multiple licensing programs for its cores.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.arm.com/why-arm/how-licensing-works|title=How Arm Licensing Works|website=Arm Holdings|access-date=29 August 2020}}</ref> Arm also offers Artisan POP IP, where Arm partners with [[Semiconductor fabrication plant|foundries]] to provide physical implementation, which allows faster [[time to market]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.anandtech.com/show/13052/arm-and-samsung-extend-artisan-pop-ip-collaboration-to-7lpp-and-5lpe-nodes  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180707010914/https://www.anandtech.com/show/13052/arm-and-samsung-extend-artisan-pop-ip-collaboration-to-7lpp-and-5lpe-nodes  |url-status=dead  |archive-date=7 July 2018  |title= Arm and Samsung extend Artisan POP IP collaboration to 7LPP and 5LPE nodes |publisher=Anand Tech|date=6 July 2018|access-date=13 February 2022}}</ref>

In February 2016, Arm announced the Built on Arm Cortex Technology licence often shortened to Built on Cortex (BoC) licence. This licence allows companies to partner with Arm and make modifications to Arm Cortex designs. These design modifications will not be shared with other companies. These semi-custom core designs also have brand freedom, for example [[Kryo#Kryo 280|Kryo 280]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.anandtech.com/show/10366/arm-built-on-cortex-license|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160531104910/http://www.anandtech.com/show/10366/arm-built-on-cortex-license|url-status=dead|archive-date=31 May 2016|title=ARM Details Built on ARM Cortex Technology License|last=Frumusanu|first=Andrei|website= anandtech.com|access-date=26 May 2019}}</ref>

Arm Holdings plc is a British semiconductor and software design company headquartered in Cambridge, England, whose primary business is the design of central processing unit (CPU) cores that implement the ARM architecture family of instruction sets. It also designs other chips, provides software development tools under the DS-5, RealView and Keil brands, and provides systems and platforms, system-on-chip (SoC) infrastructure and software. As a holding company, it also holds shares of other companies. Since 2016, it has been majority owned by Japanese conglomerate SoftBank Group.
"ARM" was originally an acronym for Acorn RISC Machine and later for Advanced RISC Machines. While ARM CPUs first appeared in the Acorn Archimedes, a desktop computer, today's systems include mostly embedded systems, including ARM CPUs used in virtually all modern smartphones. Processors based on designs licensed from Arm, or designed by licensees of one of the ARM instruction set architectures, are used in all classes of computing devices. Arm has two lines of graphics processing units (GPUs), Mali, and the newer Immortalis (which includes hardware-based ray-tracing).
Arm's main CPU competitors in servers include IBM, Intel and AMD. Intel competed with ARM-based chips in mobile devices but Arm no longer has any competition in that space (although vendors of actual ARM-based chips compete within that arena). Arm's main GPU competitors include mobile GPUs from technology companies Imagination Technologies (PowerVR), Qualcomm (Adreno), and increasingly Nvidia, AMD, Samsung and Intel. While competing in GPUs, Qualcomm, Samsung and Nvidia all have combined their GPUs with Arm-licensed CPUs.
Arm had a primary listing on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) and was a constituent of the FTSE 100 Index. It also had a secondary listing of American depositary receipts on New York's Nasdaq. However, Japanese multinational conglomerate SoftBank Group made an agreed offer for Arm on 18 July 2016, subject to approval by Arm's shareholders, valuing the company at £24.3 billion. The transaction was completed on 5 September 2016. A planned takeover deal by Nvidia, announced in 2020, collapsed in February 2022, with SoftBank subsequently deciding to pursue an initial public offering on the Nasdaq in 2023, valuing Arm at US$54.5 billion.
